extracted.intended_audience: mathematics educators, mathematics education researchers, and advanced undergraduate mathematics students
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for reading and understanding advanced undergraduate mathematical proofs, aimed at improving students' local and holistic comprehension and suggesting teachable reading strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local understanding — meaning of terms and statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowing the meaning of the terms and statements within the proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of Mejia-Ramos et al.'s model of proof comprehension: local understanding requires comprehension of vocabulary and formal statements so the reader can follow deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local understanding — justify how new assertions follow
rubrics_metrics.description: Being able to justify how new assertions in a proof followed from previous ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should be able to explain or reconstruct the logical steps that connect claims; the paper contrasts this with merely accepting steps without reasoning about their derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local understanding — relate assumptions and conclusions to the proof method
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding how the assumptions and conclusions related to the proof method being used.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This includes attending to whether the proof is direct, contrapositive, by contradiction, etc., and ensuring the proof framework actually establishes the intended implication (avoids mistaking a proof of the converse for a proof of the claim).

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — summarize high-level goals
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide a summary of the proof that emphasizes its high level goals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A holistic summary shows what the proof is trying to accomplish and how its parts serve these goals; useful for seeing the proof as a structured argument rather than a sequence of calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — apply methods in other situations
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the methods of the proof in other situations to prove new theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Holistic comprehension includes recognizing techniques that are portable to other problems (identifying novel techniques that might be useful elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — break into sub-proofs
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seeing how a longer proof decomposes into parts helps the reader grasp structure and organization; linked to Leron's notion of 'structuring' proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic understanding — apply methods to a specific example
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply the methods of the general proof to a specific example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Translating general arguments into concrete examples helps clarify abstract inferences and verify understanding of methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #1: Trying to prove a theorem before reading its proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Attempting to prove the theorem oneself before reading the given proof (e.g., 'When reading a theorem, I usually try to think about how I would prove the theorem before reading its proof').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits illustrated by transcripts: attempting a proof helps readers identify high-level goals and structure, see why the proof works, and understand employed techniques. Survey data: 88% of mathematicians preferred students use this strategy, but only 31% of mathematics majors self-reported using it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #2: Compare assumptions and conclusions with the proof technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly consider what is being assumed, what is being concluded, and what proof technique is being used when reading a proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Helps detect framework errors (e.g., proofs that actually show the converse). Transcript example shows labeling P and Q and recognizing contrapositive/direct structure. Survey data: 64% of mathematicians preferred this approach for students, but only 33% of mathematics majors reported doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #3: Break a longer proof into parts or sub-proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition longer proofs into parts or sub-proofs to understand each component's role (e.g., marking line ranges that form separate sub-arguments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students in transcripts routinely partitioned proofs (dashed lines, noting where one part ends and another begins). Survey data: 88% of mathematicians preferred students use this strategy, but only 38% of mathematics majors reported doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #4: Compare the proof approach to one's own approach
rubrics_metrics.description: After reading a proof, compare the method used to how one would have approached the problem oneself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This comparison can expose new techniques and problem-solving perspectives ('it gives you new techniques to solve proofs like that'). Survey data: 87% of mathematicians preferred students use this strategy, but only 26% of mathematics majors reported doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strategy #5: Use a concrete example to understand a confusing inference
rubrics_metrics.description: Check a new assertion by instantiating it with a numerical or concrete example to see why it is true (e.g., 'So, say 7 is a divisor of 21...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example-checking helps clarify abstract claims when readers are confused; although not a proof, examples aid comprehension. Survey data: 77% of mathematicians preferred students use this strategy, but only 43% of mathematics majors reported doing so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pedagogical goals of proofs — beyond mere conviction
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs presented to students should provide insights such as explanations of why the proven result holds true and techniques useful for other proofs; proofs that merely convince students are of limited pedagogical value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Hanna and Hersh: educators should aim for proofs that explain and reveal methods, not only convince; students who accept statements because an authority says so gain little pedagogical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Active construction to fill gaps and reveal higher-level ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers must actively construct missing steps and infer reasoning because conventional proofs often contain gaps and a linear deductive presentation that can hide higher-level ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper emphasizes that understanding requires more than literal translation of each line; students should actively reconstruct omitted inferences and seek the proof's structure and motivations.
